query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Vacuum heat treatment of the FeNiCrCoCu thin coating at a moderate temperature (around 500 °C) leads to an optimized microstructure (e.g., formation of nanotwins and fine recrystallized grains with a high density of dislocations) that increases the coating’s hardness and consequently its resistance to high‐temperature wear. In contrast, higher temperature treatments (e.g., 700 °C or 900 °C) cause grain coarsening and loss of hardness, which degrades wear resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu protective thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Subject the coating to a controlled vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear scenarios under elevated operational temperatures (up to about 500 °C) and under comparable mechanical loading conditions that simulate service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Induction of a heterogeneous microstructure with nanotwins, fine recrystallized grains, and a high density of dislocations that enhances microhardness.
generation.mechanism: The moderate heat treatment promotes microstructural refinement that increases hardness, thereby improving the coating’s ability to resist abrasive, adhesive, and oxidative wear at high temperatures. In contrast, excess heat treatment (700 °C or 900 °C) leads to full recrystallization and grain coarsening, reducing hardness and wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: When tested under high-temperature wear conditions, the 500 °C heat-treated coating will exhibit a lower wear rate, reduced spalling volume, and higher microhardness compared to both the as-deposited coating and coatings subjected to higher heat treatment temperatures.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating without any post-deposition heat treatment.
generation.boundary: Applicable for thin protective coatings operating in high-temperature regimes (up to approximately 500 °C) under mechanical loading conditions relevant to wear applications.
generation.uncertainty: While similar HEA systems (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn) show this behavior, FeNiCrCoCu-specific responses may differ slightly. The precise microstructural evolution and its quantitative impact on high-temperature wear resistance in FeNiCrCoCu coatings require experimental confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings on identical substrates. Subject one set to no heat treatment (baseline), one set to vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C, and additional sets to higher heat treatments (e.g., 700 °C and 900 °C). Conduct high-temperature sliding wear tests (simulating the intended operational load and temperature up to 500 °C) on all samples. Characterize the microstructure (using SEM and TEM), measure microhardness (via nanoindentation), and quantify wear (through wear scar volume and weight loss measurements).
measurements: Microstructural imaging (SEM/TEM for nanotwin formation, grain size)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 500 °C heat-treated sample does not show a statistically significant improvement in microhardness and a reduction in wear rate compared to both the as-deposited and higher temperature (700 °C or 900 °C) treated samples under high-temperature wear testing conditions, then the proposed mechanistic hypothesis—that the induced microstructural refinement at 500 °C governs the improved wear resistance—would be falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1. Phase Structure and Morphology of CoCrFeNiMn High-Entropy Alloy Coating
cited_evidence.text: Figure 7 shows the microhardness distribution curves of CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings prepared by CS and HVOF, and the coatings heat-treated at different temperatures. Both coatings reach the highest hardness at 500 °C, 487.6 HV0.1 for CS coating and 352.4 HV0.1 for HVOF coating. At 700 °C and 900 °C, the hardness of both coatings is lower than that at room temperature. This is because the heat treatment at 500 °C makes the coating form a heterogeneous structure composed of nanotwins in the recrystallized grains, and high-density dislocations appear in the deformation region. When the annealing temperature exceeds 500 °C, the coating exhibits a completely recrystallized structure, the yield stress decreases and the hardness decreases.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 14 shows the wear amount and wear rate of CS and HVOF coatings heat treated at different temperatures. In general, the variations of the two coatings are relatively consistent. The wear rates of the two coatings without heat treatment are very close, which are 0.2952 mm3 m−1 N−1 and 0.3016 mm3 m−1 N−1, respectively. The wear rate of the CS-500 °C coating is 0.2152 mm3 m−1 N−1, which is about 4/5 (0.2651 mm3 m−1 N−1) of that of HVOF-500 °C coating. The sliding wear resistance of the CS coating is better compared to the HVOF coating. After heat treatment at 500 °C, the hardness of the HVOF coating and CS coating increases and the internal stress decreases, so the wear resistance is better. High-temperature heat treatment (700, 900 °C) leads to grain coarsening, thus reducing hardness and wear resistance. The wear rate of the HVOF-900 °C coating is the highest, about 1.1 times that of the CS-900 °C coating. The wear volume and wear rate of the substrate are 0.0275 mm3 and 0.4534 mm3 m−1 N−1, respectively. This also shows that the coatings can protect the substrate after reasonable heat treatment.
